summary: The note reports on the Virtual Party, a political party founded on September 14, 2024 that campaigns, debates and drafts policy in virtual environments. It covers the party's milestones, from its first rally to AI-assisted policy advisors, along with its platform on digital governance, education, cyber diplomacy and environmental sustainability. It also notes the challenges the party faces, such as digital divides and privacy concerns, and asks whether its momentum can become real political clout.
one_line: The Virtual Party, founded in 2024 by Dr. Alex Sterling, uses digital platforms and AI to campaign and push a policy agenda for the digital age.
key_facts: The Virtual Party was established on September 14, 2024.
Its founder and leader is Dr. Alex Sterling, a former AI psychologist and blockchain entrepreneur.
The party's first virtual rally on October 29, 2024 drew attendees from over fifty countries.
On December 3, 2024, a bill drafted entirely in a virtual assembly of party members and digital avatars of citizens was presented to a national parliament, a first in history.
On January 15, 2025, the Virtual Party introduced its first AI-assisted policy advisors, which process vast amounts of public data to help shape policy suggestions.
Starting February 10, 2025, the party proposed an education plan overhauling curriculums to focus on digital literacy, coding and ethical technology use from a young age.
In a statement on March 8, 2025, Dr. Sterling announced the party's ambitions for 'cyber diplomacy' to settle disputes, form alliances and establish treaties in the digital realm.
The Virtual Party initiated a global digital sustainability conference on April 22, 2025 to reduce the environmental impact of digital consumption, including data centers and blockchain.
The party's campaign strategy relies on social media algorithms and data-driven outreach to send personalized messages to voters.
Its manifesto covers smart governance, digital citizenship, cyber defense, reform of outdated privacy laws, and equitable distribution of the digital economy's dividends.
Challenges include digital divides, technological accessibility, the readiness of political institutions for virtual processes, and data security and privacy concerns.
The note says it remains an open question whether the party can convert its digital appeal into tangible political clout.
